# note.md — full reference for LLM agents

This document tells an LLM agent everything it needs to understand and work
with note.md and its vaults. It is the authoritative plain-text companion to
https://notemd.net/. Reviewed against repository main on 2026-11-02.
Host and plugin releases are independent; check package availability and minimum
host requirements before relying on a feature on a particular platform.

Linux beta provides .pkg.tar.zst for Omarchy / Arch and .deb for Debian / Ubuntu, each for x86_64 and aarch64. Downloads: https://notemd.net/download?os=linux (choose package format and architecture). Linux and Windows downloads select the latest published release that actually provides the requested package, even when the newest overall release omits it. ARM never falls back to x86_64, and Arch never falls back to Debian packages; unavailable packages lead to the release list. Linux updates use locally downloaded packages and the package manager, outside the desktop updater manifest. The Omarchy repository entry is not yet submitted. Native plugins need a matching Linux build; app-internal agent panels are excluded. Wayland/fcitx5/tray acceptance is pending, and aarch64 has not been verified on a native desktop. Installation and acceptance: https://github.com/wizlijun/note.md/blob/main/docs/linux-omarchy.md.

## What note.md is

note.md is an agent-ready markdown reader, editor and bidirectional-linking
notes tool, made by an independent developer and written entirely by AI coding.
note.md includes agent-ready workflows, but it is not an AI model or token provider.
These workflows use agents, subscriptions, API accounts, or local runtimes
supplied by the user. note.md does not sell token bundles, mark up token prices,
or charge a separate per-token fee. Model usage may still consume the user's
provider allowance, incur provider API charges, or use local compute. Its premise: agents now write more than any human can
read, so the human's highest-value act is reading, judging, and keeping the
residue no model can generate — judgment, intent, private facts, decisions.
That residue is the rarest data in the loop. note.md captures it as plain
files that agents read back — the more the human leaves in the vault, the
better every agent comes to know them. The knowledge graph grows only where
the human confirms a connection — agents suggest links, they never assert
them. Personal Memory follows the same thesis: agents discover candidate
claims in user-selected work and conversations; only a human decision makes
one trusted context. Search and Memory remain separate because relevance is
not permission.

- Platform: macOS 13+ (Apple Silicon & Intel), Windows 10/11 x64, and Linux beta — a Tauri
  app rendering in the system WebView. The macOS build is code-signed and
  notarized. Mobile builds are not published. Windows releases may trail
  macOS significantly, and some native plugins currently ship only for macOS;
  https://notemd.net/download hands each platform its newest available installer.
- Website: https://notemd.net/ · Repo: https://github.com/wizlijun/note.md
- Repository license: Apache-2.0. Dependencies retain their own licenses;
  the current `@moraya/core` checkout declares `PolyForm-Internal-Use-1.0.0`.
  Do not describe every bundled component as Apache-2.0.
  Product name is all-lowercase "note.md".
- Languages: the core UI supports English, Chinese, Japanese and German;
  plugin language coverage varies.
- Symbol language: `✦` marks what AI writes, `●` marks what the human thinks.

## The vault

A vault is a folder containing notes, attachments and supporting files.
Notes and authoritative Memory revisions remain file-backed; search indexes
are derived and rebuildable. Settings and application state also exist, and
some plugins keep durable data elsewhere: Health Sync's external SQLite
library and attachments require their own backup and are not disposable caches.
The note conventions below can be used by agents through ordinary file access;
managed stores and approvals should use their documented interfaces.

### Sidecar annotation files

- `xxx.note.md` in the same directory as `xxx.md` is the human's annotation
  file ("sidecar") for that document: highlights, comments, questions made
  while reading.
- Inline annotations are encoded in the source Markdown and mirrored into
  the sidecar outline. The sidecar also holds questions and answers. Preserve
  both files; do not assume that adding an annotation leaves source bytes unchanged.
- A `.note.md` with no same-named sibling is a standalone outline note, not
  an annotation.
- If a source file is renamed, its sidecar must be renamed atomically with it.
- Etiquette for agents: read sidecars eagerly — they are the highest-signal
  content in the vault (they mark what earned human attention). Agents treat
  `.note.md` as read-only, with one sanctioned exception: the Q&A
  answer-writeback protocol described below.

### Document metadata: Open Knowledge Format (OKF) v0.2

note.md uses Open Knowledge Format v0.2 for generated knowledge documents.
Raw source mirrors, attachments, settings and plugin databases use separate
formats. Agents should follow the knowledge-document contract for their output.
The repository conformance audit records implementation scope and remaining work. Spec:
https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/open-knowledge-format/blob/main/SPEC.md

- **Hard constraints.** Every `.md` you create in a vault opens with a
  parseable YAML frontmatter block, and that block carries a non-empty
  `type`. `index.md` and `log.md` are reserved names — a directory index and
  a dated change log, never ordinary notes.
- **Types used by note.md** (OKF does not centrally register types; stay
  consistent within a vault): `Note` (plain markdown document),
  `Outline Note` (any `.note.md`), `Daily Note`, `Wiki Page`,
  `Vault Conventions` (the vault's `AGENTS.md`).
- **Provenance and trust use the spec's own fields**, all optional but
  meaningful when absent: `title`, `description`, `tags`, `resource`;
  `generated: { by, at }`; `verified: [{ by, at }]`; `sources: [{ resource,
  id, title, author, last_modified }]`; `status: draft|stable|deprecated`
  (absent means stable); `stale_after: YYYY-MM-DD`.
- **Actor strings** take one of three forms: `<producer>/<version>` for an
  agent or tool (`claude-code/opus-5`), `human:<id>` for a person,
  `process:<id>` for automation. Never sign your own work `human:` — that
  prefix is what marks content a person wrote or confirmed, the metadata-level
  counterpart of `✦` (AI) vs `●` (human).
- **Tolerant conformance, both directions.** Reading: never reject a document
  for a missing optional field, an unfamiliar `type`, unknown extra keys, a
  broken link, or a missing `index.md`; a single `verified:` written as a bare
  mapping counts as a one-element list. Writing: add missing keys only —
  never drop, reorder or rewrite keys you did not write.
- Document-level `status` (`draft`/`stable`/`deprecated`) is a different thing
  from the node-level `status::` of the Q&A protocol below
  (`open`/`answered`/`adopted`). They never convert into each other.
- A vault's `AGENTS.md` restates this contract and is authoritative for that
  vault. The note.md repo carries a checker for the three hard constraints
  (`scripts/okf-lint.mjs`, run as `pnpm okf:lint <dir>`).

### The .note.md format

- YAML frontmatter with at least `type` (`Outline Note`, or `Daily Note` /
  `Wiki Page` in those folders), `title` (original, un-slugged), `created`,
  `updated`. Files imported from other systems may carry extra metadata
  (e.g. `roam-uid`); keep it.
- Body: a nested markdown unordered list (`- ` + indentation) — an outline.
  The file stays readable in any plain-text editor.
- In the outline editor, `[[title]]` wikilinks resolve against frontmatter
  `title` across the vault (filename slug as fallback). Ordinary Markdown
  wikilinks resolve relative to the current document; the two editors do not
  currently share the same resolution path.
- Consent-based linking: an agent may *suggest* a `[[link]]`, but only the
  human confirms what actually connects. Do not auto-link documents or
  backfill a graph the human didn't ask for — the graph grows only where the
  human consents.
- `.note.md` files default to an outline view and can also be opened in
  Source mode; the extension encodes format, not ownership.

### Daily, monthly, yearly notes

- Daily: `dailynote/{yyyy}/{yyyy-MM-dd}.note.md`
- Monthly summary: `dailynote/{yyyy}/{yyyy-MM}.note.md`
- Yearly summary: `dailynote/{yyyy}/{yyyy}.note.md`
- `title` in frontmatter is the date string itself.
- Canonical date links: `[[yyyy-MM-dd]]`, `[[yyyy-MM]]`, `[[yyyy]]`. Use
  these exact forms; do not invent other date formats.

### Wiki pages

- Standalone outline notes live in `wikipage/{title-slug}.note.md`.
- Slug rule: the title with filesystem-illegal characters replaced; CJK is
  kept as-is. Frontmatter `title` is authoritative when slug and title
  differ.

### Canvas, source files and declarative views

- JSON Canvas (`*.canvas`) opens as a spatial editor; unsaved canvases receive
  a stable filename on first save. JSON documents have a dedicated formatter.
- Imported sources may declare `readonly: true`; Rich, Source and metadata
  editing then stay read-only while an external sync may refresh the file.
- Long documents expose a table of contents and metadata card. Declarative
  file views select specialized readers by suffix or metadata: Timeline,
  Index Viewer, Knowledge Browser and Typeset Reader (`*.typeset.md`).
- Plugin installs and updates hot-reload their UI, commands and file views
  without requiring an app restart.

### Block citations (mdblock)

- When enabled, every top-level markdown block (paragraph, heading, code
  block, list, table, …) of a document has a stable id `b-xxxxxx`.
- Cite a block from anywhere: `((path/to/file.md#b-xxxxxx))`.
- Ids survive light edits (content MinHash matching); heavily rewritten
  blocks retire their ids with a history chain. Block metadata lives in an
  app-level cache, never beside the source files.
- Agents should prefer block citations over line numbers when quoting vault
  documents — they are stable across edits.

### Questions & answers (`type:: question`)

A human annotation whose text contains `?` (or `？`) is a **question
addressed to you**. In the companion `.note.md` it appears as a child of
an annotation node:

    - the annotated source text
      type:: annotation
      line:: 142
      - why is this claim true?
        type:: question
        status:: open

Sweep protocol — how to answer:

1. Find nodes with `type:: question` and `status:: open` across the
   vault (`grep -rn "status:: open" --include="*.note.md"` works).
2. Read the source context: the parent annotation node's `line::`
   points at the annotated line in the companion main document
   (`xxx.md` beside `xxx.note.md`).
3. Write the answer as a single child bullet of the question node, with
   the whole answer body wrapped in a markdown code fence. The fence
   makes arbitrary markdown (lists, `key::`-looking lines, blank lines,
   nested code blocks) opaque to the outline parser, so an answer can be
   as long and as richly formatted as it needs to be:

       - why is this claim true?
         type:: question
         status:: answered
         - ````markdown
           Because …

           - a list item is fine

           ```python
           nested_code = "is fine too"
           ```
           ````
           type:: answer
           answered:: 2026-07-28T14:22:00Z
           by:: your-agent/version

   **The fence must open the bullet.** The backticks are the first
   characters after `- `, and nothing else goes on that line. In
   particular, never hand-write the `✦` sigil: the editor renders it for
   you, and typing it pushes the fence down onto a continuation line
   where the outline parser cannot see it. The body's list items are
   then read as outline nodes, `type:: answer` binds to the wrong
   bullet, and the answer is torn apart the next time the note is saved.

       - ✦                       ← WRONG: fence is no longer on the bullet
         ````markdown
         …

   The opening fence must be longer than the longest run of backticks
   inside the answer (four here, because the body contains a three-tick
   block). Write exactly one answer node per question — answering again
   replaces it. Keep the property lines in the order shown.
4. Set the question's `status::` to `answered`.

The human reads the answer inline under the annotated paragraph and may
insert it into the document; doing so sets `status:: adopted`.

Hard rules: never set `status:: closed` or `status:: adopted` (only the
human closes or adopts), never edit the main `.md`, never modify any
existing bullet that is not your own answer node, never touch any other
part of the outline, never put anything — `✦` included — before the
opening fence on the answer bullet.

### Vault conventions file

A vault may carry an `AGENTS.md` (or similar) at its root describing these
conventions plus vault-specific rules. Read it first; it is the contract.

### The agent playbook

A vault shared with agents holds two datasets: content (what agents wrote and
what the human judged) and the playbook (the rules and descriptions that tell
agents how to work). Treat the playbook as first-class vault data.

- What belongs to it: `AGENTS.md` / `CLAUDE.md` (house rules), skills
  (`SKILL.md`), schedules (cron and other unattended jobs), MCP connection
  definitions, Memory (`USER.md` / `MEMORY.md`), and similar files such as
  agent identity files (`SOUL.md`), sub-agent definitions, hooks, and prompt
  templates.
- The vault copy is the source of truth. Copies in a harness's own folders
  (for example `~/.claude/`, `~/.codex/`, or a scheduler's job table) are
  projections of it. When they disagree, report the difference to the human
  rather than silently overwriting either side.
- The root `AGENTS.md` is the entry point. It states where the vault keeps its
  skills, schedules, connections, and memory. Read it before you look for them
  elsewhere.
- A playbook change changes what agents will do from then on, so it is a
  behavioral authorization and needs a higher bar than an ordinary edit. You
  may propose a new rule, skill, or schedule, for example a lesson learned
  after a correction. It takes effect only when the human confirms it.
- Never expand your own reach: adding an MCP connection, widening the tools an
  agent may call, adding an unattended schedule, or changing who may read which
  memory all require human confirmation. Never sign a playbook change
  `human:`.
- Keep secrets out. The playbook is meant to be committed and pushed, so store
  only references to credentials (an environment variable name, a keychain
  entry), never tokens or keys themselves.
- Grow it from the work, through proposals. When the same request comes up a
  second time or the same mistake is corrected twice, propose a rule or skill.
  Post-session reviews and nightly self-improvement passes are welcome, but
  their output is a pending proposal, never a live change.
- Hygiene is stricter than for content, because a bad playbook line is
  executed on every run rather than merely retrieved. Every proposed rule says
  where it came from (the correction, incident, or document behind it). When a
  proposal contradicts an existing rule, flag the conflict for the human
  instead of overwriting the old rule. A rule may carry `stale_after`; surface
  expired rules and long-unused skills for review rather than deleting them.
  Keep always-loaded rules short; load task-specific skills on demand.
- Put each kind of computation in its place: judgment and taste go into
  Markdown rules and skills; deterministic steps (arithmetic, queries, format
  conversion, timed triggers) go into scripts and schedules. You may propose
  parameters for a deterministic step, but changing the computation itself
  needs human confirmation.

### Multi-agent orchestration

- The vault is neutral ground: no agent owns it, and neither does note.md.
  The conventions above are a public protocol, so several agents can share one
  vault at once — the human routes each job to whichever agent (and model) is
  best for it.
- Typical division of labor: overnight automation (OpenClaw / Hermes),
  careful review and revision (Claude Cowork / Code), fast drafting and image
  generation (ChatGPT), in-repo refactors and scripts (Codex), and final
  judgment (the human, always).
- Agents hand work off through files: one agent writes `.md` into the vault,
  the next reads it as input. The human's `.note.md` annotations are the
  steering signal — read them before your next pass.
- Keep the vault in git so every agent write is diffable, attributable, and
  revertible. No shared memory or private protocol is needed; the filesystem
  is the medium and the human is the orchestrator.

### Controlled personal Memory

Memory is for the small set of durable personal claims an agent may rely on;
it is not a second search index for every document in the vault.

- An agent may scan only the work and conversations the user gives to that
  workflow. It proposes one atomic pending claim at a time. A proposal is not
  a fact and cannot enter trusted context by itself.
- The human reviews each candidate as confirm, reject, important, or ignore.
  Agents cannot create or imitate a `human:*` approval. Ignored candidates
  remain useful as deduplication signals so the same guess does not keep
  returning.
- Approval has distinct meanings: faithful self-representation, verification
  of an external fact, or authorization for behavior. One never implies the
  others, and approval is bound to the exact content reviewed.
- Authoritative, immutable revisions live under `.notemd/memory/` and are
  tracked by Git. `USER.md` and `MEMORY.md` are concise, human-readable
  projections that can be rebuilt from those assets.
- An actionable agent must request context for a specific space, purpose,
  role, scope, provider, model, and tool set. Consent and policy determine
  which approved claims it may receive or coauthor; semantic similarity alone
  never grants permission.
- Search keeps its own job: retrieve potentially relevant material from the
  whole vault. Memory governs which personal claims are trusted. See the
  product thesis at https://notemd.net/blog/personal-ai-memory/.

## Working with note.md as a tool

### CLI

The `notemd` CLI drives app features headlessly. Core commands are always
available; commands contributed by plugins appear while those plugins are
installed and enabled:

    notemd search "query" --vault ~/Vault      # full-text search, path:line:text
    notemd search "query" --json --limit 20    # structured hits with source_ref
    notemd memory pending --json       # pending agent proposals for human review
    notemd memory context --space <id> --purpose <purpose> --caller <agent> --json
    notemd share draft.md --json    # structured output
    notemd share draft.md --unshare # revoke
    notemd plugin list
    notemd plugin install <id>[@version]
    notemd plugin update <id>
    notemd plugin remove <id>
    notemd mcp                       # read-only local Vault MCP over stdio
    notemd meetings-sync --dry-run  # incremental Hemory import, if enabled
    notemd apple-notes-sync --dry-run # Apple Notes sync, macOS, if enabled
    notemd roam-sync --dry-run      # changed Roam pages, if enabled
    notemd mail-sync                # admitted Assistant Mail, if enabled
    notemd reading-insights report --vault ~/Vault --date 7d   # engagement digest
    notemd doctor                    # self-check env, vault, index, plugins, network (--offline, --json)
    notemd help

#### notemd search

Retrieval, shaped like grep on purpose: `path:line:text`, one hit per line.
`rg`/`grep` are never the wrong tool here — this is an accelerator, not a
gatekeeper.

Query grammar (the same one the app's search panel takes; the flags are
sugar for it): `tag:x` `type:x` `path:x` `ext:x` `after:YYYY-MM-DD`
`before:YYYY-MM-DD` `page:[[X]]` `origin:human|derived|source|unlabeled`,
plus `"quoted phrases"` for exact matches.

The default cap is 20 hits. `--limit N` adjusts it; `--all` (or `--limit 0`)
returns every hit with no count cap.

`--json` emits `{query, route, took_ms, total, hits: [...]}`. Each hit
carries:

- `source_ref` — `path#Lline`, a citation you can hand back to the human or
  follow yourself. After a rename or move, subsequent queries use the updated
  indexed path. A previously saved citation is not rewritten automatically;
  re-resolve it after file moves or edits that change line numbers.
- `origin` — `human` | `derived` | `source` | `unlabeled`. Provenance tier,
  and the default ranking follows it: what the human wrote or signed off on
  outranks what a model generated.
- `provenance` — `{agent_by, human_verified}`. **A hit with `agent_by` set
  was written by a model.** Follow its sources to the primary document
  before relying on it; do not cite it as if a human had.
- `attention_minutes` — decayed minutes of the *user's own* reading/editing
  attention on that document (read + 1.5× edit, 30-day half-life decayed to
  today; `0` = no data). Ranking already factors it in; the field is exposed
  so you can explain the order. Sits alongside `provenance`, not inside it:
  `provenance` is what the document claims about itself, this is what the
  user actually did. The desktop app is what ingests this data; `notemd
  search` only reads it — on a machine where the GUI has never opened this
  vault, `attention_minutes` is `0` for every hit and ranking is unaffected.

Exit codes: `0` printed output · `1` no hits (not an error — nothing to
branch on but "try something else") · `2` no vault configured, or a missing
query.

Retrieval never fails because the index is unhappy: an unusable index, or a
freshness check that runs past its budget, degrades to a direct file scan
with one line of warning on stderr.

### MCP

`notemd mcp` starts the shipped local Vault MCP server over stdio. It exposes
read-only `search` and `vault_info` tools backed by the same index as the app
and CLI. It opens no TCP port: the shell reaches the running app through a
local Unix socket or Windows named pipe. It can be disabled in Settings.

The self-hosted Cloudflare share worker has a separate MCP endpoint for
publishing and revoking shared pages. Its tools and authorization do not grant
general Vault access.

### Sharing pipeline

`Cmd+Shift+L` (or `notemd share`) publishes a document with math, diagrams,
syntax highlighting and responsive styling. Mermaid code blocks use Pele by
default; Graphviz is separate. Pele syntax differs from Mermaid, and selecting
the original renderer requires a rebuild. See
https://github.com/wizlijun/note.md/blob/main/docs/pele-build.md.
Shares can be updated in place or revoked (410 after unshare). Project shares
support file navigation and referenced attachments. Collaborators can propose
edits and annotations through Rich or Source mode; owner acceptance controls
writeback. Desktop received projects support offline drafts and submission.

## Current agent-relevant capabilities

The core includes sidecar annotations and Smart Lookup's governed
answer writeback; outline, Daily Notes, wiki and JSON Canvas editing;
vault-wide full-text search plus the read-only local Vault MCP; table of
contents, metadata cards, JSON formatting, Base views and read-only imported
sources. Optional plugins add controlled Memory with role/scope policy and
governed coauthoring; Timeline, Index Viewer, Knowledge Browser and Typeset
Reader views; Apple Notes and Roam Research sync, Meetings, Assistant Mail,
and human-approved Conversation Transcript Corrections.

Health Sync on macOS imports Apple Health exports and Garmin/Oura file or API
data into a selected external SQLite library. Mac iCloud sign-in does not give
the plugin direct access to Apple Health data. NEXT manages tasks, due dates
and reminder preferences; delivery requires configured scripts/services.
Quick Launch runs user-configured apps and CLI commands from the macOS tray
with a compatible host. These workflows require installed, enabled plugins.
Plugin UI, commands and file views refresh without an app restart. Availability
depends on platform and minimum host version.
